The Imperial Ballet was the state ballet company of Imperial Russia, centered at the Mariinsky Theatre in St. Petersburg and later Moscow, that became the epicenter of classical ballet development in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Under choreographers like Marius Petipa and in collaboration with composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, it created the canonical full-length ballets Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty, and The Nutcracker, which remain the foundation of the global classical ballet repertoire. The institution's aesthetic principles, techniques, and repertoire defined what classical ballet would become worldwide.

The Imperial Ballet was established as Russia's court ballet in the eighteenth century. It evolved into a state institution with formal training, hierarchy, and canonical repertoire by the nineteenth century. The company was located primarily at the Mariinsky Theatre, originally known as the Imperial Theatre, in St. Petersburg, where it became synonymous with classicism and technical perfection.

Marius Petipa served as Ballet Master for over sixty years. He created the choreographic vocabulary and full-length ballet template that still governs classical ballet today. He collaborated with Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky on three masterworks. Swan Lake premiered in eighteen ninety-five, though it was revised after Petipa's initial contribution in eighteen seventy-seven. The Sleeping Beauty came in eighteen ninety, and The Nutcracker in eighteen ninety-two. These three works form the holy trinity of ballet repertoire.

The dancers were trained using the Cecchetti method, a rigorous codification of technique that standardized classical ballet training across Russia and influenced schools worldwide. The company's aesthetic emphasized verticality, turnout, extension, and aristocratic restraint—an ideal of the human body as an instrument of precision and grace. This contrasted sharply with the emerging modern dance aesthetic that would develop in the twentieth century.

Dancers at the Imperial Ballet achieved god-like status in Russian society. The company was a symbol of imperial prestige and artistic achievement. Though the company was dissolved during the Russian Revolution, its legacy persisted in the Kirov Ballet, the Soviet successor, and continues in Mariinsky Ballet productions today.

Marius Petipa was the choreographer who codified its aesthetic and created its masterworks. Tchaikovsky was the composer whose three ballets became its most celebrated productions. Swan Lake is the iconic work premiered in its final act by Petipa. The Sleeping Beauty was Petipa's full-length masterpiece for the Imperial stage. The Nutcracker is the holiday staple that emerged from Imperial commission and tradition. The Russian Empire was the imperial court that patronized and enshrined the company as an institution. St. Petersburg is the city that housed and nurtured the company's development.
